articles.body: Signal's screenshot block stops the button, not the agent Signal blocked screenshots in its iOS and Android apps on Friday to stop OS-level AI agents from reading your private chats. The block is real, and it is aimed at the wrong door: the agent caught reading Signal messages two days earlier got in through push notifications on Android and accessibility permissions on macOS — neither of which a screenshot block touches. What Signal actually shipped iOS 27: screenshots blocked inside Signal by default, plus a new "Block Siri AI" toggle under Settings > Privacy > App Security. Android: Signal's existing "Screen security" feature now turns on automatically when it detects an AI assistant trying to read the screen.

articles.title: US/EU Scheduling: Manual Database Polling or DLQ Redrive for Failed Job Retry?
articles.excerpt: Short answer: for a small US/EU app, start with a database polling queue when a failed job and its business record need one transaction; use DLQ redrive when retry traffic needs an isolated dispatch b…
articles.body: Short answer: for a small US/EU app, start with a database polling queue when a failed job and its business record need one transaction; use DLQ redrive when retry traffic needs an isolated dispatch boundary, and make either choice idempotent before calling it reliable. The least complex useful design is not a particular queue. It is a state machine with a stable job identity, a bounded retry policy, and evidence for every state change. A manual polling loop can implement that design, but a SELECT pending query followed by an update is not yet a queue; it has no credible answer for two workers seeing the same row, a process ending after an external effect, or a job whose failures are no longer transient.

articles.title: How to Check a Fake microSD Card with H2testw: The Full Write-and-Verify Test
articles.excerpt: A 512 GB microSD card for the price of a sandwich. Windows shows the full 512 GB, files copy onto it without complaint — and then one day your holiday photos are just gone. The only test that cannot b…
articles.body: A 512 GB microSD card for the price of a sandwich. Windows shows the full 512 GB, files copy onto it without complaint — and then one day your holiday photos are just gone. The only test that cannot be fooled by a fake card is a full write-and-verify pass, and on Windows the classic free tool for that job is H2testw. H2testw is a small, portable Windows utility from Heise, the publisher of Germany's c't magazine. It writes 1 GB test files (1.h2w, 2.h2w, and so on) until the card is full, then reads every file back and compares the contents with what it wrote. Version 1.4 is frozen and no longer developed — which does not matter, because writing data and reading it back never goes out of date as a method. Why is this needed at all?

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 21, 1676: Danish astronomer discovers speed of light — by accident — while observing Jupiter's moon Io
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of lightwhile observing Jupiter and its moon volcanic moon Io. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light . Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast. Rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io . He was trying to figure out how long it takes Io to orbit Jupiter in hopes of using it as a cosmic clock. He watched Io disappear behind Jupiter and reappear on the other side. He did this over and over every 42 hours for years. To his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the eclipses happened 11 minutes early. Likewise, when the two planets were farthest away, the eclipses were 11 minutes behind schedule.

articles.title: SpaceX will retire 1st Starship upper stage ever caught by 'chopsticks,' Elon Musk says
articles.excerpt: The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. Rather, it will go on display as a museum piece, according to company founder and CEO Elon Musk.
articles.body: The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. That vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship 's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX 's Starbase site in South Texas. Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk , who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen. "In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk said on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit .

articles.title: European-Japanese BepiColombo probe arrives in orbit around Mercury today
articles.excerpt: The BepiColombo spacecraft will finally arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet.
articles.body: Mercury is about to receive a robotic visitor from Earth. The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency ( JAXA ) — will arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet. The big moment will come after an orbit-insertion burn, which is scheduled to begin today at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT) and last for 37 minutes. BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio.

articles.body: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:20 p.m. EST (8:20 p.m. local California time; 0420 GMT on Nov. 21), on a Space Force mission called USSF-317. The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth about 8.5 minutes later, touching down in the Pacific Ocean atop the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You." It was the 11th launch and landing for this booster, which is designated B1100.
